title: Magnetomotive Force: Ampere-Turns and Gilberts
h1: Magnetomotive force units — ampere-turn and gilbert
description: MMF = NI, in ampere-turns. 1 Gb = 10/(4π) At ≈ 0.7958 At. Reluctance networks convert MMF to flux the way voltage drives current.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against NIST SP 811 and category-specific ISO references

hero: Magnetic circuits use MMF the way electrical circuits use EMF. NI in, Φ out, reluctance in between.
body: Magnetomotive force is the magnetic-circuit analogue of EMF. It is what the coil produces; the magnetic reluctance of the core determines the resulting flux.

> MMF = N × I in ampere-turns (At)
> 1 gilbert = 10/(4π) At ≈ 0.7958 At
> Φ = MMF / ℛ, where ℛ is reluctance (A/Wb)
Ampere-turn: modern SI solenoid, transformer and relay design. Gilbert: legacy CGS design texts and some older US datasheets — still used in gapped-core reluctance calculations.

A relay armature needs 800 At to pull in. A 4000-turn coil requires 0.2 A. Pull-in current ripples with battery droop — set the datasheet input in At, size the coil so operating current still delivers required MMF at end-of-life battery voltage.
MMF is NI. Convert gilberts to At by multiplying by 0.796.

faqs.q: Why is MMF not in volts?
faqs.a: It is a magnetic-circuit quantity. The analogy to EMF is dimensional, not literal.
Yes — series magnetic paths add MMF the way series EMFs add voltage.
